01-softmax.html.heading: The starting point: keep every note
01-softmax.html.where: We begin at the beginning — GPT-2's original design, before anyone had worked out how to stretch a model's memory cheaply. To see why everything later exists, you first have to see the baseline: a model that keeps a record of every single word it has read and throws nothing away.
01-softmax.html.problem: Keeping one note for every word carries two bills that both keep climbing: the room to store the notes, and the effort to read all of them again for each new word. On a short text it's nothing — a couple of gigabytes for something that fits on a laptop. On a long one — a manual, a transcript, a book — the pile swells past 260 gigabytes. And every time the model adds a word, it re-reads the whole pile to decide what matters. The effort doesn't creep up; it explodes.
01-softmax.html.idea: For every earlier word the model keeps one note — a small record of that word and its context. To choose the next word, it makes a single pass over all the notes, scoring each for how relevant it is right now, and lets the strongest ones weigh most. Nothing is discarded, so recall is flawless — as if a writer could lay every earlier sentence on the table, take them all in at once, and naturally focus on the few that matter.
01-softmax.html.term: Researchers call this full attention — the model 'attends to' (scores and weighs) every note in its memory before it acts. The name is literal: it pays full attention to everything, every time.
01-softmax.html.price: The trouble is that the re-reading grows with the square of the length: double the text and the work roughly quadruples. So the longer the document, the faster the cost races toward impossible — a hard ceiling baked into the design. The model itself also grew enormously (22,580 times larger from GPT-2 to Kimi K3), but the real bottleneck was never its width. It was always this pile of notes, and how expensive it became to carry and re-read.
01-softmax.html.aha: The baseline remembers perfectly — right up until the pile of notes becomes too big and too slow to afford, which happens far sooner than you'd think.

03-deltanet.html.heading: Erase before you write
03-deltanet.html.where: The last rung kept a single fixed-size board and blended every new fact smoothly into it. But blending had a cost: if the same label came up twice with different answers, the board just averaged them. It could not fix a fact or change its mind.
03-deltanet.html.problem: Picture a whiteboard where the marker never fully wipes off. You write 'the capital is Berlin', later learn it should be 'Vienna', and all you can do is write over the first — what's left is a smudge of both, pulled toward the middle. Ask the board later and it mumbles. In the run below, when a fact has been rewritten, the blend-only board hands back a 0.68 match to the new answer and a nearly identical 0.70 to the old one: it has forgotten nothing, and so remembers everything at once, as mush.
03-deltanet.html.idea: Instead of just adding each new fact, look first. Before writing a value under a label, check what already sits under that label, remove it, and write the new value in its place. That's not blending — it's replacement: one fact per label, and when the fact changes, the label changes with it. The board stays clear because the old entry comes off before the new one goes down.
03-deltanet.html.term: Researchers call this the delta rule — 'delta' means the difference, the change from old to new. It writes only the gap between what's stored and what's arriving. Models built around it are called DeltaNet.
03-deltanet.html.price: That cleanliness costs speed. To erase correctly you must look up the old value, work out the difference, then write — and you can't shortcut that the way you can with plain addition. So every single word needs the same careful three-step dance, which makes training slow. The board is accurate now; the price is paid in time.
03-deltanet.html.aha: A memory you can rewrite is far more useful than one that can only pile up — being able to forget the old answer is worth the extra care it takes.

04-chunked.html.heading: The same bookkeeping, reorganized to run in parallel
04-chunked.html.where: The erase-then-write method is exactly right, but it has a punishing flaw: each word has to wait for the one before it to finish, so you can't speed things up by working on many words at once.
04-chunked.html.problem: Imagine a workshop where each person can't start until the person before them hands over their piece — a single-file line where nobody moves until the slowest link finishes. Training a model means doing this across millions of words. A modern computer is built to do hundreds of things at once, but the one-at-a-time rule forbids it. The bookkeeping itself isn't slow; the waiting is. So training crawls.
04-chunked.html.idea: Inside a small block of text — say 32 words — the bookkeeping can all happen at once; you don't have to finish word 1 before touching word 2 within the block. What must still be passed in order is only a short summary from the end of one block to the start of the next. So you do each block's work in one parallel burst and hand a summary forward. The long chain of 'wait for the previous word' becomes a short chain of 'wait for the previous block' — and the answer comes out identical.
04-chunked.html.term: Researchers call this working in chunks (a 'chunk-wise' method): split the text into fixed-size blocks, do all the careful memory work inside each block at once, and pass only a brief summary between them.
04-chunked.html.price: The memory is still one fixed-size board. It can blend and correct a labelled fact, but it can't wipe itself clean when the topic changes completely — old facts will still bleed into a new chapter. Giving it a way to deliberately forget is the next rung.
04-chunked.html.aha: Re-scheduling the exact same calculation — not changing it — cut the chain of waiting from millions of words to dozens of blocks and ran 3 to 22 times faster, while the answer stayed true down to rounding noise.

05-gated.html.heading: The board learns to let go
05-gated.html.where: The board can now recognize a fact it has seen and rewrite it in place. But it has no natural way to shed old material when the subject changes — yesterday's plot details sit right next to today's, getting in the way of what the model needs now.
05-gated.html.problem: A whiteboard that never erases fills up. Old writing gets buried under new, but it's still there, and you keep having to work around it. When you switch from a mystery novel to a cooking manual, your mind doesn't instantly drop the plot — stale details linger and compete for room. The board has the same drag: it can fix a known fact, but it can't choose to let go. Write about one topic, switch to another, then ask about the first, and the old words come back loud and present even though they're useless now.
05-gated.html.idea: Add one control: a dial that sits between reading the old board and writing the new fact. Before each update, turn the dial and the whole board fades a little — not erased, just dimmed, like breath slowly clearing from a window. Turn it toward 'forget' and the board dims fast; toward 'keep' and almost nothing fades. Now when a new subject arrives, the old one wears thin on its own, making room without any special rule to detect or delete it.
05-gated.html.term: Researchers call this a decay gate (or forget gate). The idea comes from an earlier design called Mamba, which found that simply letting the board fade by a fixed fraction each step is cheaper than deciding what to keep. The fade multiplies: at a setting of 0.9 the board is 90% as vivid after one step, 81% after two, about 35% after ten.
05-gated.html.price: One dial for the whole board is still crude. It fades names and dates at the same rate as passing details — everything dims together. A fact that matters can fade too fast while noise fades too slow. You're still forcing a single pace onto every kind of memory.
05-gated.html.aha: Turn the dial down after a chapter about a wizard's tower and up before a recipe, and the old story melts away like ink in water while the new one stays sharp.

06-kda.html.heading: Each kind of thing remembers at its own speed
06-kda.html.where: We had a single forget-dial that dims a fixed-size board evenly — everything fades together. That keeps the cost flat however long the text, but it's blunt: the board treats a person's name the same as a throwaway detail, so it drops what matters just to make room.
06-kda.html.problem: Imagine listening to a mystery with one master volume knob. Turn it down to clear the background chatter and you also mute the detective's key clue; leave it up to keep the clue and you drown in noise. One dial forces all-or-nothing. In a real passage a name or a plot twist should stick for the whole stretch, while what someone had for lunch can go almost immediately — but a single dial fades them at the same rate. The board can't hold some things steady while clearing others in the same step.
06-kda.html.idea: Give every separate slot on the board its own forget-dial. Now, as each word arrives, some slots fade slowly — holding names and key facts — while others fade fast, clearing small talk. The slot tracking 'who is speaking' turns its dial down gently so that identity lives for dozens of words; a slot tracking something that resets constantly turns its dial down hard. Same fixed-size board, but now it can be selective: keep what serves the thread, drop what clutters it, all at once.
06-kda.html.term: Researchers call this per-slot (fine-grained) gating; in Moonshot's Kimi Linear model it's the core idea, named Kimi Delta Attention. Each slot simply gets its own fade-speed.
06-kda.html.price: Even with per-slot fading, a fixed board still can't recall everything that ever happened. So the model keeps a few full keep-everything layers on the side for the moments that truly need exact recall — mixing one full layer in for every three cheap ones, which is what cuts the memory bill by about 75% in the real design.
06-kda.html.aha: The moment each kind of information is allowed to fade at its own speed, cheap fixed-size memory starts to rival the expensive keep-everything kind — because matching the shape of the problem beats brute force.

07-kimi-k3.html.heading: The full picture: everything in its place
07-kimi-k3.html.where: We have built, piece by piece, a path from the simplest memory trick — a fixed-size board that blends new facts in — to a memory smart enough to keep some things and drop others at its own pace. Now comes the hardest step: putting it all together. Kimi K3 is not bigger in every direction; it is bigger only where being bigger does a job.
07-kimi-k3.html.problem: A model that remembers cheaply and also remembers exactly when exactness matters is trying to satisfy two opposite demands at once. The cheap board lets it read millions of words. But sometimes — answering a question three hundred pages in, or quoting one specific line — a blended summary of everything isn't sharp enough; it needs to reach back and touch the exact moment. And even the cheap board has to spend its extra size carefully: pour capacity in evenly and most of it is wasted. The task of assembling is really the task of placing capacity only where it earns its keep.
07-kimi-k3.html.idea: Three upgrades sit on top of the cheap memory board. First: instead of one all-purpose network, Kimi K3 keeps hundreds of small specialist sub-networks and, for each word, wakes only a handful of them — most stay asleep, so the work per word stays small even though the total is enormous. Second: the internal squashing step that keeps numbers tame is swapped for a gentler version that knows its own ceiling — it rises where the old one keeps rising, then levels off, like a volume knob that refuses to go past a limit. Third: a deep layer can reach back and pull the work of one specific earlier layer straight forward, instead of getting an equal blend of all of them — so it can fish out a precise detail from far back.
07-kimi-k3.html.term: The team of specialists is called a mixture of experts — the plain name says it all: a small router wakes just a few of them per word. The gentler, self-limiting squash is called SiTU (a bounded version of the usual squashing step). The reach-back to grab one exact earlier layer is called attention residuals. And the finished model is Kimi K3, from the lab Moonshot AI — the current frontier of this whole search for cheap, honest memory.
07-kimi-k3.html.price: This isn't the end of trade-offs; it's a smarter arrangement of them. Most of the specialists sleep, so the cost per word stays low — but you've built hundreds of them, so the model is heavy to store. The self-limiting squash never runs away, but it also never lets a value climb as high as the old one, which costs a little in rare cases. And reaching back to one exact layer is sharp, but the model has to learn which layer to grab, and that takes more training. You haven't made memory free; you've made it useful, and paid what it actually costs.
07-kimi-k3.html.aha: Kimi K3 is 22,580 times bigger than GPT-2, but the real gains came not from size alone — they came from learning exactly where each grain of that size does a job.
